content: 1. Suppression of viral load (VL) significantly reduces the probability of HIV transmission during risk acts between an infected and an uninfected individual. The degree of viral load suppression is influenced by the efficacy of antiretroviral drugs and the levels of retention and adherence among people living with HIV (PLHIV). 2. To interpret viral load data effectively, it is essential to understand the coverage of VL testing. This includes determining whether the data represents all individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) or only a subset, and identifying any biases in the data. In some settings with limited VL data, testing may be targeted at individuals showing signs of treatment failure, which can skew results toward higher viral loads. 3. Viral load data may also be biased toward more favorable outcomes, as individuals who visit healthcare facilities are often those with better retention and adherence to ART, making them more likely to achieve viral suppression. 4. Indicator values for VL metrics may be adjusted based on assumptions about the viral load levels of patients not on ART or those unaware of their HIV status. 5. There is an expected time lapse between the initiation of ART and the achievement of viral load suppression. To standardize measurement, VL data can be aggregated to assess suppression rates in a population starting six months after ART initiation. 6. Cross-sectional VL measurements, which include all individuals on ART regardless of treatment duration, provide a snapshot of overall viral suppression in a population. This can include populations on ART, those in HIV care, diagnosed HIV-positive individuals, or the broader population living with HIV. Such metrics offer insights into HIV transmission dynamics. 7. Measuring VL at specific treatment durations, such as 12, 24, or 36 months after ART initiation, allows for the assessment of disease progression and the setting of programmatic targets. 8. The definition of an undetectable viral load depends on the sensitivity of the testing method. For the purposes of VL indicators, suppression is typically defined as a viral load of less than 1,000 copies/mL. However, countries may adopt additional thresholds relevant to their context. 9. Population-level VL data is critical for evaluating the effectiveness of ART programs. Researchers have proposed several ways to express VL at the population level, including mean VL, median VL, cumulative VL, and the percentage of individuals achieving VL suppression. 10. Mean VL measures can be problematic due to the skewed distribution of VL data, often presented on a logarithmic scale. Median VL adjusts for this skew but loses significance when more than half of the population has undetectable VL. 11. Cumulative VL, which sums all VL values in a population, has been suggested as a way to characterize the absolute potential for HIV transmission within a community. This metric can distinguish between communities with large and small populations living with HIV. 12. Calculating the percentage of individuals with suppressed VL is a straightforward and intuitive measure of protection, similar to describing the proportion of people who inject drugs using sterile equipment. 13. Viral load suppression at 12 months after ART initiation is a key indicator of program performance. It measures the percentage of individuals on ART who achieve suppression (VL < 1,000 copies/mL) within this timeframe. 14. Programs should routinely collect disaggregated data on VL suppression by sex and age, and review it annually. Where routine data collection is not feasible, estimates can be derived from HIV drug resistance surveillance. 15. VL suppression is the best available measure of patient adherence to ART and reflects the ability of healthcare facilities to provide care that prevents HIV drug resistance. Good performance is defined as achieving suppression in more than 85% of patients, while passable performance is above 70%. 16. Monitoring the percentage of individuals on ART who receive at least one VL test result in the past 12 months is essential for interpreting VL suppression rates and assessing the scale-up of VL testing. 17. Population-level VL suppression, defined as the percentage of all PLHIV with suppressed VL, provides insights into HIV transmission dynamics within the overall population. 18. Early VL testing, conducted at six months after ART initiation, is a quality indicator for early assessment. VL is expected to be suppressed within this timeframe. 19. Long-term VL suppression, measured at 48 months after ART initiation, reflects the quality of care and clinical outcomes for patients managing chronic HIV disease. 20. Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) accounts for over 90% of pediatric HIV infections. Without antiretroviral interventions, the risk of transmission is 30–35%, but this can be reduced to less than 5% with effective triple antiretroviral therapy (ARV). 21. The prevention of MTCT (PMTCT) involves a comprehensive approach with four key components: primary prevention of HIV among women of childbearing age, prevention of unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV, prevention of HIV transmission from HIV-positive pregnant women to their infants, and provision of treatment, care, and support to HIV-positive mothers and their families. 22. The PMTCT cascade tracks the sequence of interventions provided to mother-baby pairs, from HIV testing during pregnancy to early infant diagnosis and linkage to chronic HIV care for mothers. 23. Recent developments in PMTCT include simplified ARV regimens and the adoption of lifelong ART for all HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women (Option B+). This approach ensures continuous treatment and better integration of ART services into maternal and child health (MCH) clinics. 24. As countries adopt these guidelines, more women are on long-term ART, often using single-pill, fixed-dose combination drugs. Health systems have adapted by decentralizing services, task-shifting, strengthening supply chains, and enhancing laboratory capacity at MCH clinics. 25. Data collection for PMTCT must align with ART monitoring systems to ensure compatibility and long-term follow-up, particularly in settings where lifelong ART is provided.
